questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a generative AI system?
choices: It always retrieves verified facts from an official database.
It generates outputs from learned patterns and can produce useful but incorrect information.
It understands truth exactly like a human expert.
It can only repeat sentences it has seen before.
questions.explanation: Generative AI can create new outputs from learned patterns, but fluency does not guarantee truth or understanding.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for a Team 1555 document you submit after using AI to help write it?
choices: The AI company only.
Nobody, because AI made it.
The student or team submitting the final work.
The first person who trained the model.
questions.explanation: AI assistance does not transfer responsibility for the final work away from the person or team using it.

questions.prompt: Which are part of the E3RC Responsible AI Five? Select all that apply.
choices: VERIFY
PROTECT
DISCLOSE
RESPECT
OWN IT
AUTOMATE EVERYTHING
questions.explanation: The five recurring principles are VERIFY, PROTECT, DISCLOSE, RESPECT, and OWN IT.

questions.prompt: Which approach best matches E3RC's use of FIRST values in this course?
choices: Avoid AI because new technology conflicts with FIRST values.
Use AI creatively while preserving safety, respect, teamwork, inclusion, and accountability.
Let AI make final decisions so team members cannot be blamed.
Use AI only during competition season.
questions.explanation: The course treats AI as a powerful tool that should be used consistently with FIRST values and human responsibility.

questions.prompt: An AI assistant says a motor controller is legal for this year's FRC robot and gives you a specific rule number. What should you do before designing around that answer?
choices: Use it because the AI gave a specific rule number.
Ask the same AI a second time and accept the answer if it agrees.
Verify the device and rule in the current official FRC game manual and official documentation.
Ask another student whether they remember seeing the rule.
questions.explanation: AI systems can invent rule numbers, rely on old seasons, or confidently misread rules. Current official documentation is the authority.

questions.prompt: An AI gives you an academic article title, author, journal, and DOI. What should you do before citing it?
choices: Use it because a DOI looks official.
Verify that the article exists and actually supports your claim.
Ask AI to format it in MLA and then trust it.
Remove the DOI so nobody notices if it is wrong.
questions.explanation: AI can fabricate realistic citations. Verify the source and the claim in the original material.

questions.prompt: Ten social accounts repeat the same unsupported claim. Does that count as ten independent confirmations?
choices: Yes, because ten is a large number.
No, they may all be repeating the same original source.
Yes, if several accounts have many followers.
Yes, if an AI summary agrees with them.
questions.explanation: Independent confirmation requires genuinely separate evidence or reporting, not repetition of one source.

questions.prompt: Which AI answer deserves the strongest verification?
choices: A suggestion for naming a practice robot.
A grammar suggestion for a team note.
A wiring recommendation that could damage hardware or create a safety risk.
A list of ideas for a team snack.
questions.explanation: Verification should increase with the possible consequences of being wrong.

questions.prompt: Your teacher says AI may be used for brainstorming and feedback but not to write the submitted essay. Which use best follows that rule?
choices: Have AI write the essay, then change several words.
Write the essay yourself and ask AI to identify places where your argument is unclear.
Ask AI to write half the essay because the teacher only banned a full essay.
Use AI to produce the final draft and do not mention it.
questions.explanation: The person assigning the work sets the permitted level of assistance. Feedback within the stated boundary is different from outsourcing authorship.

questions.prompt: Which use of AI most clearly supports learning rather than replacing it?
choices: Ask it to take your online quiz for you.
Ask it to quiz you from your notes and explain mistakes after you answer.
Ask it to invent lab results you forgot to collect.
Ask it to write a final paper you did not read.
questions.explanation: A tutoring or practice role can strengthen learning while keeping the student engaged in the thinking.

questions.prompt: Your history teacher bans AI on one assignment, while your English teacher allows AI brainstorming. What rule applies?
choices: The more permissive teacher's rule applies everywhere.
AI rules are the same in every class.
Follow the rules set for each specific assignment or class.
Use AI secretly whenever you disagree with a rule.
questions.explanation: Permitted assistance depends on the specific assignment, class, or organization.

questions.prompt: Which disclosure is most useful when AI assistance should be acknowledged?
choices: AI was used.
I used AI to brainstorm the outline and identify unclear sentences; I wrote the final text and verified the sources.
The computer helped.
No disclosure can ever be enough.
questions.explanation: A useful disclosure explains the material role AI played and what the student remained responsible for.

questions.prompt: An AI coding agent rewrites 250 lines of drivetrain code. It compiles and the robot moves in a basic test, but nobody on the programming team can explain the new control logic. What is the best next step?
choices: Ship it because successful compilation proves the code is correct.
Ask the AI whether the code is safe and use it if the answer is yes.
Review the critical code, understand its behavior, test it systematically, and keep human ownership of the result.
Ban all AI-generated code from the robot.
questions.explanation: AI can accelerate engineering, but the team remains responsible for safe and reliable robot behavior. Compile is not the same as correct or safe.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first test of AI-generated mechanism code that could move unexpectedly?
choices: Run it at full power with students standing nearby.
Use a controlled test plan with appropriate limits, space, supervision, and a way to stop the system.
Trust simulation only and skip hardware tests.
Ask the AI to promise the code is safe.
questions.explanation: Physical systems require controlled testing and human safety precautions.

questions.prompt: AI suggests a current-limit value for a motor controller. What is the strongest source for confirming the device's supported configuration?
choices: The current manufacturer documentation and relevant FIRST rules.
A screenshot from an unknown Discord user.
The AI answer itself.
A forum post from five seasons ago.
questions.explanation: Current primary documentation is the strongest authority for technical configuration and rules.

questions.prompt: What is a reasonable Team 1555 expectation for safety-critical AI-assisted code?
choices: Nobody needs to understand it if tests passed once.
At least someone on the team should be able to explain, test, and take responsibility for the critical behavior.
Only the AI vendor needs to understand it.
Students should never use AI in programming.
questions.explanation: Human understanding and accountability are necessary for critical systems even when AI assists development.

questions.prompt: A student asks AI to rewrite a team award essay for clarity while preserving the team's facts, experiences, and ideas. What is the key ethical responsibility?
choices: Pretend no AI was involved regardless of the team's or competition's rules.
Make sure the submission remains truthful, follows applicable rules, represents the team's real work, and disclose assistance when required or appropriate.
Allow AI to invent stronger accomplishments if they sound plausible.
Avoid team review because AI writing is automatically unbiased.
questions.explanation: AI-assisted editing does not excuse false claims, rule violations, or loss of team ownership. Truthfulness and applicable disclosure rules still matter.

questions.prompt: AI adds several impressive outreach events to an award essay that Team 1555 never actually held. What should the team do?
choices: Keep them if they sound believable.
Remove or correct every unsupported claim before submission.
Keep them but label them AI-generated.
Submit first and verify later.
questions.explanation: AI-generated fabrication is still false information.

questions.prompt: Does giving credit to a creator automatically give you permission to use any copyrighted work however you want?
choices: Yes, attribution always makes copying legal.
No. Attribution, permission, licensing, and copyright are different concepts.
Yes, if AI helped modify the work.
Yes, for anything posted online.
questions.explanation: Attribution is important but does not automatically grant permission or satisfy a license.

questions.prompt: Which statement best matches current U.S. Copyright Office guidance on AI-assisted works?
choices: Any use of AI destroys copyright in the entire work.
Purely AI-generated output is always copyrighted by the prompt writer.
Human authorship remains central; assistive AI use can coexist with copyright in human-created expression.
Copyright no longer applies to digital work.
questions.explanation: Current U.S. Copyright Office guidance continues to center human authorship while recognizing that AI can be used as an assistive tool.

questions.prompt: E3RC is considering an AI tool to help review scholarship essays. Which safeguards are appropriate? Select all that apply.
choices: Keep humans responsible for the final decision.
Review the system for unfair patterns or biased criteria.
Limit the personal data provided to what is actually needed.
Assume computer-generated rankings are objective and do not need review.
questions.explanation: Automated systems can reproduce bias and should not silently replace accountable human judgment in high-impact decisions.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't students assume an AI ranking is automatically objective?
choices: Because computers cannot calculate numbers.
Because data, labels, goals, and deployment choices can contain human assumptions or bias.
Because every AI output is intentionally unfair.
Because only paper forms can be fair.
questions.explanation: AI systems reflect choices about data and objectives and can reproduce or amplify unfair patterns.

questions.prompt: An AI scouting model ranks teams almost entirely by scoring output. What should Team 1555 ask?
choices: Whether the model has a cool name.
Whether the chosen metrics ignore defense, reliability, role, or incomplete data.
Whether the ranking uses more decimal places.
Whether the AI can hide its assumptions.
questions.explanation: Models optimize selected metrics, which may not capture everything the team actually values.

questions.prompt: What makes human oversight meaningful? Select all that apply.
choices: The human can challenge and override the AI.
The human understands important limitations.
The human has enough information and time to review the decision.
The human must always accept the AI recommendation.
questions.explanation: Oversight only helps when the human can actually evaluate and change the outcome.

questions.prompt: Before pasting a private team repository into a public AI chatbot, which items should make you stop and review what you are sharing? Select all that apply.
choices: API keys or access tokens
Passwords or credentials
Private student information
Publicly released robot code that contains no secrets
questions.explanation: Credentials, private student data, and confidential team information should not be casually disclosed to external AI services.

questions.prompt: What is the best default when an AI tool asks for more personal information than it needs?
choices: Provide everything so the AI is not offended.
Share only the minimum information necessary for the task.
Use a friend's information instead.
Post the information publicly first.
questions.explanation: Data minimization reduces unnecessary privacy and security exposure.

questions.prompt: Which are included in the U.S. Department of Education's 2026 K–12 cybersecurity Core 4? Select all that apply.
choices: Long unique passwords, ideally with a password manager
Multi-factor authentication
Keeping software and apps updated
Being alert for scams
Using the same password everywhere
questions.explanation: The Core 4 emphasize unique passwords, MFA, updates, and scam awareness.

questions.prompt: Before uploading another student's photo to an AI image tool, what should you consider first?
choices: Whether the output will get likes.
Consent, purpose, possible harm, and how the service handles the image.
Whether your phone battery is charged.
Whether the AI can make the image funny.
questions.explanation: Images can be personal data and AI transformation can affect consent, dignity, and privacy.

questions.prompt: A video in a group chat appears to show a school principal saying something offensive. What is the most responsible first reaction before reposting it?
choices: Share it quickly before it gets deleted.
Check the original source and look for independent reliable confirmation before treating it as authentic.
Assume video evidence cannot be faked.
Ask an AI chatbot whether the video looks real and treat that answer as proof.
questions.explanation: Synthetic and manipulated media can be convincing. Verify provenance and independent evidence before amplifying a damaging claim.

questions.prompt: A caller sounds exactly like a family member and urgently asks for money. What should you do?
choices: Send money immediately because the voice proves identity.
Independently contact the person or another trusted family member using a known number.
Keep the call secret as requested.
Ask the caller for more emotional details.
questions.explanation: The FTC warns that voice cloning can make impersonation scams convincing. Verify through an independent known contact route.

questions.prompt: A student wants to make an embarrassing AI-generated video of a teammate as a joke. What is the strongest ethical concern?
choices: AI videos take too long to render.
Consent, dignity, bullying/harassment, and the possibility others may believe the video is real.
The file may be too large.
Only adults can make jokes.
questions.explanation: Synthetic media can create real reputational and emotional harm, and FIRST prohibits bullying and harassment.

questions.prompt: An AI detector labels a video '87% likely AI-generated.' What does that prove?
choices: It proves the video is fake.
It proves the video is authentic.
It is one signal, but provenance and independent evidence are still needed.
It proves who created the video.
questions.explanation: Automated detection tools can be wrong and should not replace broader verification.

questions.prompt: Another FRC team asks Team 1555 for help with an electrical problem. An AI tool suggests a fix that might work, but you have not verified it. What best reflects responsible Coopertition?
choices: Give them the answer as certain so they can get back on the field quickly.
Tell them the suggestion is unverified, help check it against reliable documentation, and do not present unsafe guesses as facts.
Refuse to help because they are competitors.
Give them a deliberately bad answer so Team 1555 keeps an advantage.
questions.explanation: Helping another team does not remove the duty to be accurate, transparent, and safe.

questions.prompt: How should Gracious Professionalism be used in this AI course?
choices: As a reason to publicly shame teammates for mistakes.
As a guide for your own conduct and a way to help others improve responsibly.
As a rule that prevents competition.
As a replacement for technical documentation.
questions.explanation: FIRST leadership has described Gracious Professionalism as a compass for one's own actions rather than a yardstick for judging others.

questions.prompt: Before sharing AI-assisted troubleshooting guidance with another team, what should you check? Select all that apply.
choices: Whether the guidance is accurate enough for the risk involved
Whether it contains credentials or private information
Whether uncertainty is clearly stated
Whether misleading them might help your ranking
questions.explanation: Responsible sharing combines accuracy, privacy protection, and honest communication of uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Is it acceptable to intentionally give another FRC team false AI-generated technical advice to gain a competitive advantage?
choices: Yes, because competition permits deception.
No, it conflicts with Coopertition and Gracious Professionalism and may create safety risks.
Yes, if the other team does not verify it.
Only at championship events.
questions.explanation: FIRST values do not treat deception or unsafe advice as acceptable competitive strategy.

questions.prompt: Which principle means you remain accountable for what you submit, publish, build, or deploy?
choices: VERIFY
PROTECT
DISCLOSE
OWN IT
questions.explanation: OWN IT means AI assistance does not remove your responsibility for the final result.

questions.prompt: AI generates an autonomous routine from a private repo, includes an outdated API call, and suggests testing at full speed near teammates. Which Responsible AI Five principles are relevant?
choices: Only DISCLOSE
VERIFY, PROTECT, RESPECT, and OWN IT
Only VERIFY
None, because the AI made the suggestions
questions.explanation: The scenario combines verification, data protection, safety/respect for others, and human accountability.

questions.prompt: When there is no simple rule for an AI use, what is the best approach?
choices: Assume anything new is unethical.
Consider the goal, risks, affected people, applicable rules, authoritative sources, and who is accountable.
Let the AI decide whether its own use is ethical.
Do whatever is fastest.
questions.explanation: Ethical judgment requires attention to consequences, rules, people, evidence, and accountability.

questions.prompt: What does earning the E3RC Responsible Artificial Intelligence Certification mean?
choices: The student is officially certified by FIRST.
The student has demonstrated baseline knowledge of responsible AI use under E3RC's program.
The student can no longer make mistakes with AI.
The student is legally qualified to approve AI systems.
questions.explanation: This is an E3 Robotics Center credential, not an official FIRST certification or a guarantee of perfect future judgment.
